name: Wayfarer frames

lead: Wayfarer frames are a trapezoidal, thick-rimmed style introduced in 1952 and worn as sunglasses or prescription glasses. They add a defined brow line and frame the eyes, which is why people use them to sharpen the upper face.

The silhouette has been fashionable in several decades, from 1950s musicians to 1980s film product placement and a late-2000s revival. Fit advice is a matter of style guidance rather than published trials.

paras: People wear them as everyday sunglasses or as optical frames in acetate or similar plastic, in black, tortoiseshell or coloured finishes. Sizes vary, and the original design was later made smaller and less angular.
Eyewear carries no special hazards beyond ordinary fit and lens quality; sunglasses are commonly chosen for UV protection, which depends on the lens rather than the frame shape.

chain: Thick trapezoid frame with strong top line
angle.text: The wide top edge and angled sides add visual weight around the eyes, which is how wearers use the frames to create definition. Fit across face shapes is generally discussed in style guides rather than studies.

lead: Wayfarer frames are eyewear with a distinctive trapezoidal outline, wider at the top than the bottom, and a heavy brow line. The original, designed in 1952 by Raymond Stegeman for Bausch and Lomb's Ray-Ban brand, used then-new plastic molding technology [1].

People use them to frame the eyes and add structure to the face; original advertising described the look as "masculine" [1]. The style was worn by Buddy Holly, Roy Orbison and James Dean in the 1950s and 60s, declined in the 1970s, then rebounded after a 1982 product-placement deal and Tom Cruise's use in Risky Business (1983) [1].
Wikipedia reports that the brand was sold to Luxottica in 1999 and that the original model (RB2140) was reintroduced in 2007 after vintage pairs were worn by celebrities [1].

paras: The classic frame is trapezoidal with a thick upper rim and angled sides. A 2001 redesign made the frames smaller and less angular and moved from acetate to injected plastic [1]. The original frames' tilt made them hard to keep perched on the head, which the redesign addressed [1].

Introduced in 1952, the model was nearly discontinued in the 1970s, then boosted in the 1980s: a 1982 placement deal and Risky Business pushed sales to 360,000 pairs in 1983 and later about 1.5 million a year [1]. Chloe Sevigny and Mary-Kate Olsen wearing vintage pairs preceded the 2007 reissue [1].

timeline.event: Raymond Stegeman designs the Wayfarer for Ray-Ban [1]
